pos: n. (proper name; a Shaalbonite among David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew 'Elyachba, commonly read God will hide or whom God hides, from 'el (God) with a root meaning to conceal or to shelter.
biblical_def: Eliahba is named twice, in the two parallel rolls: “Eliahba the Shaalbonite, of the sons of Jashen, Jonathan” (2 Samuel 23:32), and “Azmaveth the Baharumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite” (1 Chronicles 11:33). He came from Shaalbim, a town of the Danite allotment that Israel had been slow to clear of Canaanites. His name is a confession worth a soldier having: God will hide — that is, God will shelter and conceal the man He means to keep. For a man in David's wars that is not sentiment but doctrine. The psalms David wrote in those same years say the same thing in full: “For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me” (Psalm 27:5). The thirty were not kept because they were hard men, though they were; they were kept because God hid them. The dictionary marks the combination the roll everywhere displays — genuine valour resting on an acknowledged dependence. Men whose faces were like the faces of lions (1 Chronicles 12:8) bore names like God will hide, and saw no contradiction in it.

corruption_summary: Courage and dependence are treated as opposites; David's roll pairs lion-faced men with names confessing God's shelter.
corruption_paragraphs: The age divides the brave man from the dependent man, so that trusting God reads as a substitute for competence and competence reads as a substitute for trust. The rolls of David's men refuse the division. These were soldiers who crossed Jordan in flood and fought lions in pits, and their names say God will hide, God hath helped, the LORD is my God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faith is the ground of courage rather than its alternative. “In the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me” (Psalm 27:5) was written by the captain these men followed, in the years he was hunted. A man who knows he is hidden by God can afford to stand in the open.

pos: n. (proper name; son of Ur, among David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew 'Eliphal, commonly read God hath judged or whom God judges, from 'el (God) with a root for judging or pleading a cause. The margin of 1 Chronicles 11:35 offers the variant Eliphelet.
biblical_def: Eliphal is named once: “Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur” (1 Chronicles 11:35). The parallel roll in 2 Samuel 23:34 gives the corresponding place in the list to “Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite,” and the margin of the Chronicles verse notes both variants. The dictionary records the difference without alarm. Two rolls of the same company, compiled at different times and perhaps from different musters, will differ in some names and patronymics; the Masoretic text preserves what it received, and nothing doctrinal depends on which form stood in the original register. What the name says is worth more than the spelling: God hath judged. In David's mouth that was the whole ground of his cause. He would not stretch out his hand against Saul and said so in the words of a man content to be judged rather than to judge: “The LORD judge between me and thee, and the LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee” (1 Samuel 24:12). A man of that company named God hath judged carried his captain's doctrine in his name.

corruption_summary: Variant names in parallel musters are urged as proof the text is unreliable; the variation touches no doctrine at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Where 2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11 differ in a name or a father's name, the difference is regularly presented as evidence that the records are untrustworthy. The dictionary holds providential preservation and reads the difference as what it is. Two musters of one company, taken at different dates, will not match name for name, and the Masoretic tradition hands down both with the margins noting the alternatives.

The principle to recover is a doctrine of Scripture strong enough to be honest. The Bible's authority does not rest on the claim that no name was ever written two ways; it rests on God's preservation of His word, which the marginal apparatus serves rather than threatens. A reader who demands a text with no variants will end by distrusting the text he has.

pos: n. (proper name; a Gadite captain, and a Korhite porter)
etymology: Hebrew 'Elzabad, God hath given, from 'el (God) and a root meaning to bestow or endow — the same root behind Zabad and Zebedee.
biblical_def: Elzabad is the name of two men. The first is a Gadite who crossed to David in the stronghold: “Johanan the eighth, Elzabad the ninth” (1 Chronicles 12:12) — ninth in a list of eleven captains of whom the chapter says that the least was over a hundred and the greatest over a thousand, and that they swam the Jordan in flood to reach him. The second is a Levite of the house of Obededom: “The sons of Shemaiah; Othni, and Rephael, and Obed, Elzabad, whose brethren were strong men, Elihu, and Semachiah” (1 Chronicles 26:7), a porter in the temple service. A soldier and a doorkeeper share a name meaning God hath given. The dictionary draws the obvious lesson from the pairing: the same word covers the gift of a captain's strength and the gift of a porter's post, and Scripture praises the Levite's brethren as strong men in the same breath in which it assigns them a gate. “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17). The man who held a thousand and the man who held a door had received alike.

He records the Gadite captains who swam a flooded Jordan and the Korhite porters who kept the gates with the same care, and he applies the same word — strong men — to the doorkeepers' house.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every capacity is received, so no office is self-made and none is beneath notice. “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17). Two men named God hath given, one commanding a thousand and one keeping a door, are the Chronicler's way of saying so.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite who came to David at Ziklag)
etymology: Hebrew 'El'uzai, commonly read God is my strength, from 'el (God) and a root meaning strength or refuge.
biblical_def: Eluzai is named once: “Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite” (1 Chronicles 12:5). The men of this list are Benjamites — Saul's own tribe — who left the king of their blood and came to David while David was still a fugitive. The chapter notes their skill with an almost affectionate precision: they were armed with bows and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows (1 Chronicles 12:2). And it records the moment of their reception, when the Spirit came upon Amasai and he answered for them all: “Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse” (1 Chronicles 12:18). To go over to David then was to risk everything on a promise not yet visible, and to do it against the pull of tribe and kin. Eluzai's name says where a man finds the nerve for that: God is my strength. The dictionary notes the chapter's summary, which reads like a quiet verdict on them all: “there came to David to help him, until it was a great host, like the host of God” (1 Chronicles 12:22).

corruption_paragraphs: Tribal and ethnic solidarity is widely treated as the deepest and most natural of loyalties, and modern identity frameworks make it nearly the only one. 1 Chronicles 12 records men of Benjamin leaving a Benjamite king for a Judahite fugitive, against every pull of kinship, because they judged that the LORD had chosen him.

The principle to recover is that allegiance to God's anointed outranks the claims of blood. “Thine are we, David, and on thy side, thou son of Jesse” (1 Chronicles 12:18) was said by men whose cousins were in Saul's army. Christ says the same thing more sharply, that a man must love Him above father and mother; and a tribe is no greater claim than a father.

pos: n. (proper name; David's overseer of field labour and tillage)
etymology: Hebrew 'Ezri, my help, from 'ezer (help) with the first-person suffix — the same root as in Ezra, Azariah and Eliezer.
biblical_def: Ezri is named once: “And over them that did the work of the field for tillage of the ground was Ezri the son of Chelub” (1 Chronicles 27:26). He appears in the register of David's civil officers, a list that is easy to pass over and quietly remarkable. After the captains of the host and the rulers of the tribes, the Chronicler sets down who managed the king's practical estate: Ezri over the ploughland, others over the vineyards, the wine cellars, the olive and sycamore trees, the oil, the herds in the valleys and in Sharon, the camels, the asses, the flocks. A whole paragraph of agricultural administration, each department with a named man over it. The dictionary notes the implication. The kingdom of the LORD's anointed included a man responsible for the tillage of the ground, and Scripture thought his name worth preserving next to the names of men who killed lions in snow. Work with soil is not a lesser calling in a book that opens with a garden and a command to dress and keep it. “Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Colossians 3:23).

corruption_paragraphs: A division between sacred and secular work runs deep in religious thinking and has no footing in this book. The Chronicler, compiling the officers of the LORD's anointed, gives a full paragraph to the men over the ploughland, the vineyards, the oil and the herds, and names each one. The kingdom had farms, and the farms had foremen, and the foremen are in Scripture.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of ordinary vocation. Man was put in a garden to dress it and to keep it before the fall, so labour is not a penalty but an original calling, and the curse touched its difficulty rather than its worth. “Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord” (Colossians 3:23) covers the tillage of the ground, and Ezri is its Old Testament instance.

pos: n. (proper name; a captain of hundreds in Jehoiada's covenant)
etymology: Hebrew 'Elishaphat, God hath judged, from 'el (God) and shaphat (to judge) — the root behind shophetim, the Judges.
biblical_def: Elishaphat is named once, and in a scene of great danger: “And in the seventh year Jehoiada strengthened himself, and took the captains of hundreds, Azariah the son of Jeroham, and Ishmael the son of Jehohanan, and Azariah the son of Obed, and Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri, into covenant with him” (2 Chronicles 23:1). Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, had destroyed the royal seed and reigned six years; one infant, Joash, had been hidden in the house of the LORD by the priest Jehoiada and his wife. In the seventh year Jehoiada brought five officers into covenant, and together they produced the king: “Then they brought out the king's son, and put upon him the crown, and gave him the testimony, and made him king” (2 Chronicles 23:11). Note what was handed to the boy along with the crown: the testimony, the book of the law. A king under a book, not above it. And the covenant Jehoiada then made was threefold — between himself, the people and the king, “that they should be the LORD'S people” (2 Chronicles 23:16). Elishaphat's name means God hath judged, and in that year God judged the house of Ahab through five captains and a priest.

corruption_paragraphs: Modern government assumes the state as the fountain of law, answerable to procedure but to no higher text. The coronation of Joash is the opposite picture: the crown and the testimony were given together, and a covenant was made between priest, people and king that they should be the LORD'S people. The king is installed under a standard he did not write and cannot amend.

The principle to recover is the lordship of Christ over the civil sphere and the accountability of rulers to God's law. The dictionary holds the three God-ordained authorities — family, church, and state — each within its own proper sphere and all under Scripture. Jehoiada did not make the priesthood the government; he crowned the rightful heir and put the law in his hand.

pos: n. (proper name; Jehu's captain, who cast Jehoram into Naboth's field)
etymology: Hebrew Bidqar, of uncertain meaning; a reading as son of stabbing or with piercing has been proposed from the elements, but nothing in the text settles it.
biblical_def: Bidkar is named once, and the verse is a memory shared between two soldiers: “Then said Jehu to Bidkar his captain, Take up, and cast him in the portion of the field of Naboth the Jezreelite: for remember how that, when I and thou rode together after Ahab his father, the LORD laid this burden upon him” (2 Kings 9:25). Years before, Elijah had met Ahab in Naboth's stolen vineyard with a sentence from the LORD, and Jehu and Bidkar had been riding behind the king that day and heard it. Now Jehoram the son of Ahab lay dead with Jehu's arrow through him, and Jehu told his captain where to put the body: in that field. The dictionary marks the mechanism. God's word spoken in a vineyard was carried for years in the memory of two young officers, and when the hour came one of them reminded the other, and the sentence was executed on the exact ground. “Surely I have seen yesterday the blood of Naboth, and the blood of his sons, saith the LORD; and I will requite thee in this plat” (2 Kings 9:26). A murdered man's field; a stolen vineyard; a king's corpse. Nothing was forgotten, and nothing was approximate.

corruption_summary: Delay in judgment is read as its absence; the word spoken in Naboth's vineyard was executed on that ground years later.
corruption_paragraphs: A sentence not carried out at once is taken for a sentence never meant, and the comfort of the wicked rests on it. Naboth was murdered for a vineyard, Ahab was told what would come of it, and years passed in which nothing visible happened. Then two men who had been in the saddle that day put a king's body on that exact plot of ground.

The principle to recover is the precision and patience of divine justice. Naboth had refused on covenantal grounds — the inheritance of his fathers was not his to sell — and his murder was answered in the place where it was committed. The God who waits is not the God who forgets, and Bidkar exists in Scripture as the man who remembered on cue.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite who came to David at Ziklag)
etymology: Hebrew Be'alyah, the LORD is lord or Jah is master, from ba'al (lord, master) with the divine element -yah — a name that takes the word used of the Canaanite god and claims it for the LORD.
biblical_def: Bealiah is named once: “Eluzai, and Jerimoth, and Bealiah, and Shemariah, and Shephatiah the Haruphite” (1 Chronicles 12:5). He was one of the Benjamites, Saul's kinsmen, who joined David in his outlaw years. His name repays attention more than most. Ba'al was the ordinary Hebrew word for a lord, an owner, a husband — and it was also the name of the Canaanite god. Bealiah's parents took that word and bolted it to the covenant name: the LORD is lord. The compound is a polemic. It refuses to surrender a good word to an idol, and insists that whatever mastery Baal claims belongs in fact to Jehovah. Later, when the name had become too compromised to use, Hosea records that God would remove it from Israel's mouth altogether (Hosea 2:17). But in David's day a man could still be named the LORD is lord and mean it as a challenge. The dictionary commends the instinct: the answer to a word captured by error is often to take it back, and the deeper answer is always to confess who is in fact Lord.

corruption_summary: Words captured by error are often surrendered; Bealiah's name takes 'lord' back and gives it to the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: When a good word is seized and corrupted, the common instinct is to abandon it, and much ground has been given away that need not have been. The name Bealiah shows the other course: ba'al meant lord, an idol had taken the word, and a Hebrew father fastened it to the covenant name as a confession. Hosea shows the limit of the strategy, for a word can become so soaked in a false meaning that God Himself removes it.

The principle to recover is that lordship is not a contested question but a settled one. “The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof” (Psalm 24:1). Elijah's challenge on Carmel put it as a choice because the people were behaving as though it were one; the fact was never in doubt. Whether a word is reclaimed or relinquished, the confession must be made.

pos: n. (proper name; a Levite musician at the bringing up of the ark)
etymology: Hebrew 'Aziel, a shortened form of Jaaziel, read God is my strength or whom God strengthens, from a root for strength with 'el (God).
biblical_def: Aziel is named once: “And Zechariah, and Aziel, and Shemiramoth, and Jehiel, and Unni, and Eliab, and Maaseiah, and Benaiah, with psalteries on Alamoth” (1 Chronicles 15:20). The occasion is David's second attempt to bring the ark to Jerusalem. The first had ended in disaster at the threshing-floor of Nachon, where Uzza put out his hand and died, because the ark had been carried on a cart after the Philistine manner instead of on the shoulders of Levites as the law commanded. David's own verdict afterward is the key to the whole chapter: “we sought him not after the due order” (1 Chronicles 15:13). So the second attempt is done by the book — Levites sanctified, poles on shoulders, singers appointed by name and by instrument, Aziel among those with psalteries. The dictionary marks this as one of Scripture's clearest lessons in worship. David's first procession had sincerity, enthusiasm, and music; what it lacked was obedience, and sincerity did not cover the lack. God is to be worshipped in the way He has appointed, and the appointing is His business and not the worshipper's.

For because ye did it not at the first, the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order.
And David spake to the chief of the Levites to appoint their brethren to be the singers with instruments of musick, psalteries and harps and cymbals, sounding, by lifting up the voice with joy.
Thus all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the LORD with shouting, and with sound of the cornet, and with trumpets, and with cymbals, making a noise with psalteries and harps.
corruption_summary: Sincerity is treated as sufficient in worship; David learned at Uzza's death that God must be sought after the due order.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing assumption of much modern worship is that God accepts whatever is offered in earnest, so that form is a matter of taste. 1 Chronicles 13 and 15 together dismantle it. David's first procession was joyful and well-meant and killed a man, and David himself diagnosed the reason: “we sought him not after the due order” (1 Chronicles 15:13).

The principle to recover is the regulative principle of worship: what God commands in His worship is required, and what He has not commanded is not ours to introduce. The dictionary holds this as the Reformed and confessional position. Note that the corrected procession was not less joyful — shouting, cornet, trumpets, cymbals, psalteries and harps — but it was joyful in the way God had appointed, with Aziel at his psaltery where he was told to be.

pos: n. (proper name; one of the sons of Zattu in Ezra's reformation)
etymology: Hebrew 'Aziza, from a root meaning strong or mighty — hence strong one. The same root gives Uzziah, Uzzi and Azaz.
biblical_def: Aziza is named once: “And of the sons of Zattu; Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, and Jeremoth, and Zabad, and Aziza” (Ezra 10:27). He stands in the register of those who had taken wives of the peoples of the land and who separated from them when the law was read. His name means strong one, and the chapter shows what strength was required — not the strength to keep what he had taken, but to give it up. The whole assembly had answered Ezra with a loud voice, “As thou hast said, so must we do” (Ezra 10:12), and then the names were taken down house by house. The dictionary notes that this is the Bible's usual location of strength. “He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city” (Proverbs 16:32). The men of Ezra 10 took no cities. They did something considerably harder, under the plain word of God, with their names written down so that it could not be denied afterward. A man called strong appears in Scripture at the moment he submitted.

corruption_summary: Strength is measured by what a man can hold; Scripture measures it by what he will surrender at God's word.
corruption_paragraphs: The world's account of strength is capacity to impose and to retain, and a culture formed by it reads submission as weakness by definition. Ezra 10 supplies the counter-case in a register of names. Men described by the chapter as trembling at the commandment of God gave up what they had taken, and the Bible writes their names down as the honourable party.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that self-rule under God's word is the true strength. “He that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city” (Proverbs 16:32) is the standard, and it finds its perfection in Christ, who had legions at His disposal and did not call them. A man named strong one is remembered for yielding.
